key_insight: Time-resolved 4D velocity measurements reveal that laminar thermal plumes in high-Prandtl-number convection do not evolve independently, but instead undergo interacting pathways such as merging, splitting, branching, pulsing, and detachment.
engineering_relevance: These plume-interaction dynamics provide a quantitative benchmark for mantle-convection and other viscous thermal-transport models, improving interpretation of hotspot and geochemical anomaly patterns.
method: 4D time-resolved volumetric velocity measurements in a high-Prandtl-number Rayleigh-Bénard system
Temperature-dependent viscosity to mimic Earth-like viscous convection
Spatiotemporal analysis of dozens of coexisting plume morphologies and interaction modes
evidence_signal: The study analyzes tens of plumes over time and reports measurable trends in plume spacing, initiation times, isolated-plume fraction, and morphology evolution.
watch_item: The conclusions are drawn from a controlled laboratory Rayleigh-Bénard system, so direct scaling to the mantle requires careful consideration of geophysical parameter differences.
paper_title: Morphology, interactions, and evolution of laminar thermal plumes revealed by time-resolved volumetric velocity measurements and analysis: Application to Earth's mantle
